member of the commission. – mr president, let me start by thanking the two rapporteurs, david martin and antonio lópez-istúriz white, for the good work they have done and the long journey that we have travelled jointly, which has brought us to where we are today. few places symbolise the benefits of trade and investments like singapore. singapore’s determination in embracing openness and globalisation has transformed a city state without natural resources into one of the most prosperous countries in the world and has helped its people prosper too. singapore has become a model of economic transformation and a prime example of how trade, investment and sustainable development can and should go hand in hand. embracing openness has served the eu well in the past, too, and still shines a light on the way forward as we discuss the issues facing us today. close partners for decades, the eu and singapore have decided to seal our partnership through the three agreements that we are talking about today and that you will vote on tomorrow. the new eu-singapore partnership and cooperation agreement will lay down the overall framework for bilateral political cooperation between two like-minded partners. but we are also very close investment and trade partners. singapore is currently our largest trade and investment partner in south-east asia and among our top 20 trading partners for goods, our top five for services and our top ten partners for foreign direct investment. the trade and investment agreements between the eu and singapore will provide a framework for these already strong flows to develop further. the benefits of the trade agreement are many. tariffs on bilateral trade will be removed. non-tariff barriers on eu exports for cars, electronics and renewables we’ll do away with. access to service procurement markets will be improved, and all this will create opportunities for businesses and for individuals on both sides. the agreement further contains a comprehensive trade and sustainable development chapter that includes obligations in relation to international conventions on workers’ rights and the environment; covers areas like biodiversity, eco-labelling and corporate and social responsibility; and gives a strong role to eu and singapore civil society groups in making sure that these commitments are put into practice. ratification of, and compliance with, international labour organisation (ilo) fundamental conventions will figure among priority items to focus and deliver on. we need to see sustained efforts in this respect, as of the agreement’s entry into force. and here already the singaporean authorities have shown good engagement in preparing for the implementation of the agreement’s sustainable development provisions. the trade agreement was also negotiated together with an investment protection agreement that contains the fully reformed investment protection system developed at eu level, which the european parliament requested and helped to shape – and i would like to thank you for this support. this system addresses the concerns civil society has expressed about vaguely defined rules, lack of transparency, absence of appeal, lack of independence of adjudicators and lack of accountability in bilateral investment agreements that we have today. so, delivering on the negotiating mandate, the commission has presented for consent an agreement that tightens the standards on investment protection so as to prevent abuses, an agreement that fully safeguards a government’s right to make new laws to protect health, the environment and other public interests. it thus establishes a fully transparent investment court system, a system which, in the very recent opinion of the advocate-general in relation to a trade agreement with canada, has been considered fully compatible with the eu treaties. that is a stepping-stone towards the multilateral investment courts that could potentially cover all 3 000 existing investment agreements worldwide and could play a central role in the future development of investment policy, including a possible evolution to include investors’ obligations, as mr martin mentioned. so these trade and investment agreements negotiated with singapore are state-of-the-art agreements with a privileged bilateral trade and investment partner to the eu. and, beyond being a partner, singapore is a beating commercial heart of the south-east asian region so, in that sense, the agreement will constitute a benchmark for negotiation with other association of southeast asian nations (asean) partners. lastly, on the partnership and cooperation agreement, this is, of course, a stepping stone towards enhanced political and economic involvement between the eu and singapore, as well as the whole region. it provides a basis, as the rapporteur mentioned, for effective bilateral engagement with singapore, strengthening the political dialogue and enhancing cooperation in a variety of areas – human and labour rights, justice, security, connectivity, people-to-people links, the information society, education and cultural exchanges, as well as employment and social affairs. it will enable us to step up scientific and technological cooperation in areas such as energy, environment, the fight against climate change, protection of natural resources, smart cities and transport. under this agreement, a joint committee will be established comprising representatives of both sides at an appropriately high level to ensure the proper functioning of the agreement and see that it is implemented. it will also set priorities and make recommendations to promote the agreement’s objectives. on regional dynamics, singapore has advocated regional multilateralism in south-east asia and is currently the country coordinator for eu-asean dialogue relations. we value that partnership very much and we are committed to ensuring that it will become even stronger. the collaboration with singapore on asean-related matters has been very fruitful so far. cooperation between singapore and the eu is already deep and wide today and, given the challenges that we are jointly facing, the potential for even greater engagement is significant – founded on a shared vision, a rule-based multilateral system and effective multilateralism. so thank you to the european parliament for the work that has been done here. we are looking forward to strong support in tomorrow’s vote.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the basis of the proposals contained in the white paper on growth and employment. the european union, after the vacuum left by the united states, is establishing itself as the absolute protagonist on the global trade scene. our third way of doing business, as opposed to protectionism as it is to unbridled liberalism, has never been so attractive. through this partnership, we are able to project our standards and values globally. the clauses on the protection of workers, consumers and the environment help us to protect citizens from the side effects of globalisation. to name a few, i refer to the commitments singapore has made to ratify the conventions of the world labour organisation, to respect the paris climate agreement, but also to recognise our geographical indications, such as pdos and docs. not only that: we cannot forget that over 90 percent of global economic growth in the coming years will take place outside our borders. these agreements therefore provide a key outlet to support employment and growth. singapore is the gateway to the asean region in southeast asia, the world's most dynamic economic region: i am not talking about the big multinationals: over 80% of european companies in singapore are small and medium-sized enterprises. exports to singapore have generated 33 billion euros in turnover for our companies. the agreement, by increasing these numbers, will create thousands of jobs in europe and at what cost? no, singapore's economy is totally complementary to the european one: from industry to agriculture, no sector of our economic system is in competitive conflict with singapore. in the face of these facts, these figures, we must have no doubt: these agreements are crucial for european workers, whose products are sold and appreciated all over the world, and for citizens, who will receive greater protection against the possible negative side effects of globalisation.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have heard how good and beneficial the eu-singapore free trade agreement can be. it seems incredible to me: the european union is a major player in the world economy, and it is a major player in the world economy. the truth is that this agreement was negotiated in an era that is far removed from the present reality. singapore, as described in the proposed trade agreement, is a hub in the south east asian region. the real risk, ladies and gentlemen, is that the advantage of this treaty will be taken by other actors who are not part of the european union and who do not respect the parameters set for trade deals. statistics show that singapore is the third largest source of counterfeit goods in the world. there are no guarantees to combat this phenomenon, which is very common in asia and of which italian industry is one of the main victims. we risk opening the door to low-cost, low-priced products from malaysia, china or indonesia, which in singapore only see the last stage of processing. many doubts also remain about protected geographical indications. the system in force in singapore does not provide for the existence of a register. our geographical indications will not be automatically protected, but european operators will have to activate the procedures themselves. singapore is also a global financial centre and the mutual liberalisation of financial services is one of the main aims of the agreement, but it could make it possible to circumvent european regulations in this area. some employee associations place singapore on a grey list of global tax havens, and the agreement provides few guarantees about tax exclusion and profit shifting for eu-based multinationals.

author of the book. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, every day thousands of women are fighting the battle against the disease of the century, cancer. they do this while bravely continuing to care for their families, while trying to keep working through it all. we are calling for easier and cheaper access to diagnostic and preventive tests and treatment for them and for everyone. the figures eurostat gives us every year are alarming: one in three europeans will develop cancer during their lifetime. some 600 000 european women die of cancer every year, of which over 90 000 are from breast cancer, as well as from uterine and cervical cancer, to name just a few. we know that cancer is devastating to everyone, men, women and sadly also children, but it must be recognized that when it strikes us women, it often strikes us in our femininity, attacking our bodies and depriving us of those parts that physiologically make us feel female, such as the breasts or the reproductive system, and from which arise enormous psychological repercussions that are often sidelined or underestimated in comparison to the severity of the disease itself. compared with the numbers of those fatally affected by the disease, fortunately many more are women who manage to overcome it. over 80% of european women with breast cancer, for example, survive after treatment. and it is these women too that we must protect, them and their families. after the illness, in fact, their lives change radically, whether due to invasive treatments, such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy, or as a result of the surgeries they are forced to undergo, with devastation not only physical - think of a hysterectomy or a mastectomy - but also psychological. we therefore urge the european commission, in conjunction with the member states, to put in place health policies and programmes which take account of a much wider range of aspects behind this terrible disease. there are three main points i would like to make. the first is the aspect of prevention, monitoring and access to care. there is no doubt that the high mortality rate from cancer is due to the fact that it is often intervened at an advanced stage of the disease, rendering all possible treatment futile. we know that if a disease is diagnosed early, the cure rate is much higher. prevention is essential through constant and affordable monitoring, including from an economic point of view, with both generic and specific screening. prevention is not always easy to implement, as the monitoring visits are often costly and the waiting times are very long. we therefore urge that work be done on this issue to protect the health of all. the second aspect is related to the specificity of the care needed in the event of women's illness. we are talking about cancers that affect exclusively female organs, such as the breast or the uterus, and that can go on to infect the femininity of the woman herself. the treatment must take into account that it is an intervention on organs and parts of the body which represent our femininity and should, as far as possible, take into account the aesthetic aspects as well as the functional ones. the last aspect, but this is the one i would like to focus on, is the psychological and welfare aspect. this is linked to the need to ensure adequate support and assistance for women. at a time when women's bodies are being attacked to fight disease and surgical operations are permanently impairing the most essential parts of our femininity or our reproductive capacity, often irreversibly, psychological assistance, even in the post-operative period, is absolutely necessary and must become a right of all. leaving these women alone means making it much more difficult for them to carry out their roles as mothers or wives, roles that certainly do not end with the illness. i would like to conclude by asking the commission to work towards a uniform european strategy for all member states, through cancer screening programmes, combined with increased investment in both research programmes and health infrastructure.

first concerns social sustainability. i have visited many of our member states, and i have seen that there are those which are advanced in social dialogue between employees and employers about how to reskill people already in jobs; and there are those which, basically, have not done anything. i am afraid this issue may become a new dividing line in europe. there are countries which understand that we have to pay more attention than before to re-skilling. there are also countries that pay more attention than others to the quality of teacher training and education internally. if member states – our governments and the social partners – don’t take more seriously the challenge of skills and the quality of basic education, then we cannot be successful. this is my first message. i believe that education – training and reskilling people – is the most important social factor in relation to sustainability. then, looking at the economic angle, i would like to mention the circular economy, including product-design policies and sustainable finance – those three concrete issues. they are the issues which, i believe, matter most with regard to improving sustainability. i had a discussion with several representatives of financial institutions, who are pleading with us to create a clear taxonomy and a classification of sustainable finance. they are saying that their clients are asking for more sustainable assets. and this is exactly what the commission is working on at the moment. we have to let the financial sector act to change the world. they are willing to do it, because their clients, us, and consumers are asking them to do it. so, if we manage to create sustainable finance criteria and a taxonomy, i’m sure that hundreds of billions of euro will shift direction and this, honourable members, will change the world, including through the circular economy. the private sector is leading the show here at moment, and this house has been extremely supportive and innovative, supporting too the developments in product-design policy because we, as consumers, are asking for more sustainable business models, more sustainable ways to consume and more durable and repairable products. so i am not worried at all about whether we can achieve the sustainable development goals, if we just manage to pick the right things to change and also, especially, if we keep the private sector onboard – because it’s not only us, as legislators or regulators, who can change the world. it’s also private operators. our role is to create a better playing field, a more sustainable regulatory environment, which will enables us and other stakeholders to do the trick. i believe we can combine social equality, social sustainability, environmental sustainability and sustainable economic growth in the future, and it should not be rocket science!

an agreement to be reached so smoothly and swiftly. tolling is a precious instrument for making the ‘users and polluters pay’ principle a reality for road infrastructure. but it has to be used in a fundamental problems in the field of electronic tolling. let me recall just its two main objectives. first, regarding the rights and obligations of market actors, it will clarify the grey zones which, so far, have been hampering the commercial deployment of the european electronic toll service (ets) in certain member states. more balanced and realistic requirements will lead to more competition on the ets market and more efficient operations. this will mean savings for road users, savings for toll chargers and additional revenues for member states. life will also be made easier for road users, in particular transport companies. they should ultimately be able to pay tolls, wherever they go in europe, with a single on-board unit. they should have to sign only one toll-service contract and should receive a single invoice at the end of the month. second, the agreed text will introduce a mechanism to facilitate the cross-border enforcement of toll payment. today, member states have no effective instruments in place to identify the owners of a foreign-registered vehicle for the purpose of toll collection. it is already possible for national authorities to go after those who commit a road-safety-related traffic offence but those who evade toll payments can escape fines. we have calculated that this leads to a revenue leakage of around eur 300 million per year. clearly, toll evasion is one of the main obstacles to a wider deployment of barrier-free tolls in the union. in addition, the agreed text extends the scope of application of the directive to tolling systems using automated number-plate recognition as the main technology. this is important to keep pace with the technological development on the ground, as stressed by the rapporteur. lastly, the co-legislators have extended the scope of application of cross-border enforcement. it will apply to all types of road fees, both electronic and manual. the commission can only support this extension. this initiative will help in the transition from traditional vignette schemes, and tolls with barriers, to modern and smart, free-flow tolling systems, the kind of systems we need in order to shape more sustainable mobility in the future. overall, i believe that all three eu institutions can be very satisfied with the outcome of the negotiations and i’m looking forward to tonight’s debate.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the commissioner, mrs salini and the shadow rapporteurs for the excellent work they have done. it is also in the small things that europe must be perceived as united by its citizens, and having a single and interoperable tolling system at union level simplifies movement in the territory and is therefore essential. efficient transport networks are essential to the competitiveness of our economies and to the success of the internal market. road transport continues to increase and the potential of the road network needs to be fully exploited. using a single piece of equipment not only allows users to interface with all systems in different countries, but also facilitates the cross-border exchange of information on infringements relating to the failure to pay a toll. for these reasons i am in favour of a european toll system which will simplify the procedures for paying at the ticket offices, thus also reducing traffic.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate mr salini and all the other members on the excellent result of the trilogue. the text under vote improves the exchange of information on vehicle data, ensures easier access for suppliers to the toll collection market and facilitates the use of a single on-board tele-tolling device for all road journeys within the european union. a mechanism for mutual assistance between member states for the enforcement of road tolls at cross-border level is provided for, but legal arrangements involving local authorities need to be put in place to better address the problem of cross-border enforcement of penalties for failure to pay tolls. finally, the issue of privacy: the introduction of electronic toll systems has implications for the confidentiality of personal data, as they can be used to generate comprehensive travel profiles. to avoid this, member states will have to provide for anonymous and encrypted prepayment options for the european parcel delivery service.

out by customs administrations in your report. as the report notes, it is vital that the customs union ensures the competitiveness of european business, especially the smes, while at the same time protecting the eu’s revenue sources and allowing the flow of goods at our external borders. balancing these objectives is the main goal of the union customs code (ucc). the ucc has been the main legal framework for customs rules since 2016 and it aims to eliminate paperwork and fully automate all customs processes. it also provides for a greater electronic integration between the member states and it facilitates trade by speeding up customs control. i welcome the reference made in the report to the major progress already achieved over the last 20 years in the digitalisation of our customs processes. the current work is about building and expanding on the existing well—functioning electronic systems. for that reason, the ucc electronic work must proceed carefully, step by step. the new systems will only replace the old ones when they have been fully tested and when they can be launched easily with no disruption to trade. thanks to the provisional agreement reached in trilogue on the proposal to amend article 278 of the ucc, the commission and member states will have the time necessary to complete their work on the 17 ucc electronic systems. most systems will in fact be completed by the previously established deadline of 2020. however, for some of them it is necessary to allow extensions up to 2022 for the three national systems and up to 2025 for six trans—european systems. we have proposed these extensions to the commission to allow traders and member states to prepare in an efficient way. we believe that the work can now proceed in a smoother way in line with a carefully calibrated and agreed timeline. and, as you request in your report, i can assure you that the commission’s work programme for the customs it projects will be regularly updated to take account of the new deadlines. and, besides, we will of course regularly inform parliament of the progress of the customs electronic projects through regular reports. greater transparency here is, of course, in everybody’s interest: for you, for the economic operators and for the general public. the commission already produces annual reports in a technical format on the multiannual strategic plans suggestions you made in your report and we intend to address all the customs issues highlighted by this house.

member of the commission. – mr president, i’m glad to join you today for this plenary debate on the european solidarity corps. this programme is still quite young but it is growing quickly and young people across europe are keen to get involved. the european solidarity corps has the potential to become another iconic programme like erasmus. solidarity among citizens and member states is one of the key values on which our union is built. the european solidarity corps offers young people opportunities to live that solidarity and to experience what being european feels like, and they are eager to take these opportunities. one hundred and thirteen thousand young people have now signed up for this initiative. almost 12 000 of these have already started their solidarity activities. this proves that the programme is responding to a clear demand on the ground. young people are making a real difference, supporting individuals and whole communities in need. this is why, in june 2018, the commission proposed to continue and further expand the european solidarity corps under the next multiannual financial framework. we want to keep the main thrust of the current programme, but extend its scope after 2020 so that we can also support humanitarian aid operations beyond the eu’s borders. i want to express my thanks for the great dedication with which the rapporteur – ms šojdrová –, and the shadow rapporteurs have taken this work forward. i would also like to thank ms theocarous for her work as the rapporteur in the development committee, particularly looking at the new humanitarian aid operations. the commission welcomes the strong support of the european parliament for the proposal and takes note of the amendments that it put forward. i am very pleased to see that we have common ground on almost all aspects of the programme. one important point where we differ and where we still need to find agreement is the new humanitarian aid stand and, more specifically, your wish to open it up to people of all ages. let me underline that the european solidarity corps is a youth programme, designed specifically to offer fresh opportunities to the young generation, to invest in their development, their skills, their dreams, and the idea is to bring all of these opportunities together in one place. in fact, the activities of the programme are limited to young people aged up to 30 for good reason: to help them in their transition to adulthood and independence and to the labour market, while obtaining a solidarity experience. thirty is not an arbitrary age limit; it is based on evidence. above this age, the vast majority of people have settled in their professional and private life. the demand is already high in the age group up to 30. removing the age limit would mean taking away opportunities for young people and we risk job substitution. moreover, the activities falling under the new humanitarian aid strand will account for only 4 500 of the 350 000 opportunities that we want to offer under the european solidarity corps over 7 years, and only 500 of these are expected to be taken up by people above 30. introducing different eligibility criteria for such a small share of activities would lead to disproportionate extra administrative costs and make the programme more complicated, threatening to shut out those who we want to benefit most: young people. i would therefore plead with you to keep the european solidarity corps a real youth programme. having said this, the commission would be keen to start negotiating with you right away, as is the council. this is my personal commitment and offer to you. i’m ready to work with you towards an agreement before the end of the current parliamentary term. partial first reading agreements have already been reached for quite a number of future programmes. it would be a pity if the european solidarity corps, this new flagship programme for young people, were to be left behind. i am sure that the good compromise we reached on the current regulation only very recently would greatly facilitate negotiations. a swift agreement would help the commission to make all the preparations to ensure that the programme can be fully and effectively implemented right from the start of 2021, but most importantly, it would send a clear signal to europe’s young generation that investing in them remains a priority for us, and that we want to do what we can to enable them to make the most of their lives and build a better europe for the future.
i think it is very important that we send a signal to the european citizens, two months before the european elections. two very powerful messages. the face of europe is also definitely that of voluntary work, solidarity and active citizenship. and this must once again be a watchword of the european union, especially from the younger generations. we must make this experience, which was already under way in the past few years and which included the european voluntary service, which, however, involved a hundred thousand young people in twenty years, permanent over the next seven years. we certainly want to be bolder. with tomorrow's vote on the establishment of the european solidarity corps, for which i was the shadow rapporteur in the s&d group, we are taking an important step forward because we are going to establish a stable union programme in the next mff and i hope that the council of ministers will accept the proposal - also in terms of the budget - that parliament has made. it will devote almost the entire budget (almost 86%) to volunteering, active citizenship and solidarity activities for young people between 18 and 30 years old, 8% of the share will go to internships and jobs, but always in the context of non-profit activities, and 6% will go to humanitarian aid, collecting an important legacy, without an age limit similar to the other. it is a political step, and we really need to tell young people who don't know about it. i think it's important to think about the fact that, symbolically, this is going to be of tremendous significance. i remember. i met them, as the commissioner did, in norcia, after a terrible earthquake: a core of young volunteers coming from 12 countries had a huge meaning. more than 70 000 young people have already registered on the dedicated online portal; 7 000 are already participating in activities on social inclusion, integration of migrants, support for local communities and cultural heritage. it is important that the appropriation for the next seven years be increased to more than one billion, confirming as a political priority this fundamental value of the european union, to respond above all to the needs of society, of the communities, promoting the personal and professional development of young people, civic, with particular attention to the most disadvantaged. that's why we wanted to make it more inclusive, for children with fewer opportunities, for example those with disabilities, health conditions, difficulties in the field of education or coming from a migrant background or from marginalized communities. i am very pleased that some very important points have been taken up. the first is the european dimension of the experience: all these activities must be transnational, not overlapping national voluntary schemes, but rather supporting countries that do not have the need to do so. the country's activities must also have this transnational dimension. and then, most importantly, we extended to social enterprises and also to private organizations, but always for non-profit activities and with the possibility of having a quality label for different types of insertion. i conclude by saying that this is a new experience that brings together the best of the past, but that also wants to have the will to build a citizenship from below. i think we need to talk a lot about this today, about institutional reforms in europe, political integration and building processes of active citizenship.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the text approved by the committee on culture defines solidarity as a sense of responsibility on the part of all, towards all, to commit themselves to the common good, which is expressed through concrete actions without expecting anything in return. with the european solidarity corps, the european union achieves the dual objective of promoting solidarity as a value, mainly through volunteering, and of increasing the participation of young people as a means of contributing to strengthening social cohesion, solidarity, democracy, european identity and active citizenship in the union and abroad. the objectives of social inclusion introduced by the european parliament are broadly shared, through a clear definition of young people with fewer opportunities, including disability, and a solid and significant component of learning and training during volunteering, useful for the performance of subsequent professional activities. that's a good sign. thousands of young people aged 18 to 30 will thus have the opportunity to engage in solidarity projects through volunteering, internships and work.
in writing. solidarity is at the heart of the european project, as enshrined in the treaties, and must therefore be preserved and fostered. the european solidarity corps is a programme which goes in this direction and therefore is undoubtedly to be appreciated and enhanced. it offers a real opportunity for young people to grow, both personally and professionally, by helping local communities in need. specifically, i would have preferred that only non-profit organisations could participate in the programme, to avoid, for example, possible abuses by multinationals who do not need public money to clean up their image. the so-called employment part (crafts and jobs) also leaves me a little puzzled, as it risks degrading a noble activity such as volunteering and favouring low-cost labour replacement practices. fortunately, my proposals have succeeded in increasing the safeguards and protections, introducing a clear demarcation line between voluntary and work activities, and introducing strict control procedures to exclude from the programme organisations which have broken the rules. we cannot allow the high unemployment rates, caused, among other things, by draconian austerity policies, to justify in any way the exploitation of our young people.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it took almost 10 years of debate, 20 countries to legislate on the subject, but above all the insistence of this parliament and our two resolutions, the last of which (for which i thank vice-president mairead mcguinness once again) was overwhelmingly approved in june 2016: it took all this to get to the final vote today on the directive against unfair trading practices in the agri-food chain. it is an extraordinary achievement, made possible by the leadership and ambition of this parliament. this ambition has been realised in crucial improvements over the initial proposal. just to name a few: the extension of the scope, which now covers 100% of farmers and more than 95% of agri-food businesses in the union, with a turnover of eur 50 million to eur 350 million; the inclusion of buyers based outside the union among those who will have to comply with the directive; the inclusion of all agricultural products and not only food, protecting strategic sectors such as livestock farming and animal feed, pet food; strengthening and doubling the number of prohibited practices from 8 to 16, including, for example, late payment for non-perishable products, refusal to grant written contracts, or the threat of commercial retaliation in the event of denunciation; the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the situation in the community. the obligation to act and to put an end to unfair practices for national law enforcement authorities, to whom we have also granted greater powers both in the investigative phase and in terms of sanctions; the commission will also be able to provide information on the implementation of the directive, without forgetting the enhanced cooperation between the various national authorities, which will have to meet at least once a year and exchange information and good practice in order to ensure the most uniform and ambitious possible application of the directive. it is worth remembering that this is a minimum harmonisation and that the member states will be able to provide in their national legislation both the extent of the parties involved and the list of unfair practices to be prohibited. in order to achieve this, ladies and gentlemen, in the 11 months since the commission's proposal was published, despite the various attempts to block this directive once again, it has taken a strong political will on the part of everyone. i would therefore like to thank all those who have made this possible, starting, of course, with my colleagues in the commission, starting with commissioner hogan, whom i thank, the shadow rapporteurs, the whole negotiating team of the european parliament, the services, the austrian presidency, minister elisabeth kostinger, president-in-office of the council, without forgetting the fundamental work done by all the technical groups and of course also by my team. president. - ladies and gentlemen, this directive is europe showing that it is able to stand by the weakest economic operators, such as farmers, and all citizens. a supply chain characterised by unfair behaviour and thus by an inefficient distribution of resources puts all producers under pressure, in a race to lower prices that depresses both the quality of the products that reach the tables of households and citizens and the quality of the production process, encouraging labour exploitation and unsustainable production practices. on the contrary, by overcoming these distortions within the agri-food chain, the directive will be a reference point for achieving more transparent and fair markets, more efficient markets capable of generating benefits for society as a whole, and in particular for consumers.
i am glad that the commissioner has taken the initiative to put forward a proposal for a directive on unfair trading practices in the food chain. i am glad that the commissioner has taken the initiative to put forward a proposal for a directive on unfair trading practices in the food chain. the number of unfair practices is increasing significantly, with eight more practices than the commission proposal, ranging from last minute cancellation of orders to late payments, from unilateral changes to contracts to non-payment to suppliers for unsold goods by large central purchasing agencies. one of the strengths is undoubtedly the anonymous report in defence of the confidentiality of the supplier during the investigation procedure not only with regard to his identity but also to all other information that the supplier himself identifies as sensitive. the rules contained in the directive finally restore dignity to european agriculture by strengthening the position of producers vis-à-vis large retailers.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the rapporteur for the good work he has done. the adoption of the unfair commercial practices directive is a major milestone, so that we can finally have a fairer redistribution of economic value in the agri-food chain, so as to guarantee a better income for small farms, but also a better quality of products available for sale. this directive is an act which is necessary to restore balance to the commercial chain by providing protection for those who, because of their small size, are too often at risk of being crushed by the abuses of larger players. the lack of bargaining power forces many small businesses to sell their products under unfair terms, to make economic agreements that impoverish them and to take on the costs and risks of doing business for others. clear rules at european level now unambiguously condemn all commercial practices by unscrupulous economic operators which end up crushing honest small farmers. once and for all, unfair trading practices such as unilateral and retroactive changes to supply contracts, commercial retaliation and payment for services not rendered will be stopped and punished. we are giving the member states an important and effective tool. if these rules are properly applied, they will restore fairness and dignity to small businesses, the weakest links in the agri-food chain.
mr president, mr de castro, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption of the directive on unfair trading practices in the food sector is a first step which is not enough to recognise the fact that: the eu has built an internal market full of imbalances, starting with those between mainly agricultural suppliers and commercial buyers. we are thus trying to mitigate unfair behaviour between those who have a de facto dominant position and suppliers, who often remain outside the sales mechanisms, witness auctions at a discount and promotional contests, and are often illegitimately asked to pay for some of the measures for the sale and storage of their products. today, in italy, we share with apprehension the fate of the sardinian sheep and goat breeding sector, which is not only committed to revolutionizing its own aggregating model and making the mechanisms governing the pdo pecorino romano more efficient, but also to defending itself against certain unfair behaviour by some buyers who try, even through a transfer price that is too low in relation to production costs, to maintain a distance from farmers on the distribution of the final value. we therefore strongly support this measure, in the hope that the next legislature will take care to introduce new rules for the internal market so that the right value can be given to agricultural products throughout europe, respecting the different realities and the different production costs.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to express my great appreciation for the tenacious, valuable and effective work of my colleague, mr de castro. the text agreed with the council on the proposal for a directive on unfair trading practices in business-to-business relations in the food chain is a fundamental and necessary instrument. in a market-oriented agricultural policy context, good and fair management of the food chain has become of key importance, in particular for small farmers, who are particularly vulnerable to unfair trading practices, as they often lack the same contractual power as their partners who buy their products. this is mainly due to the limited alternatives they have to get their products to the final consumer, as well as the structural weaknesses of the agricultural system. the directive aims to tackle unfair trading practices by introducing common protection instruments across the european union, including a more extensive list of prohibited practices. the objective to be achieved, and i assure you that i shall vote in favour of it, is to help ensure a fair standard of living for the farming community, thereby achieving one of the main objectives of the cap. i believe that this is a legislative measure of great importance also for italian and sicilian farmers in particular.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, agricultural policy is a pillar of the european union and provides massive financial support to farmers and producers, but unfortunately, more and more often, together with trade policies, it is being attacked, because our farmers are being crushed by disparate labour costs, structural shortcomings and the overpowering power of large-scale distribution, which imposes unfair trade practices. the weakest links in the chain are thus the ones who fail, and they often react by attacking europe itself, and us who represent them. with this directive we are finally demonstrating in practice which side we are on: the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council and the european parliament, and to be adopted by the council and the european parliament, and to be adopted by the european parliament, and to be adopted by the council and the european parliament. from tomorrow this will be possible, thanks to the effective work of our vice-president de castro, the commission and all those who, like myself, have always fought for the farmers and small producers, the symbol of our agri-food industry.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome this directive, which after so many years will finally protect farmers from unfair practices by purchasing and distributing companies and bring about a better balance throughout the food chain. i would like to point out the specific case that happened in sardinia - the region from which i come - and i would like to express my full solidarity with the situation. i hope that this directive will restore fair rights to all the thousands of workers who have unfortunately worked without them and i hope that these rights will be recognised.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr de castro. farmers and agri-food producers, as we know, are unfortunately vulnerable to unfair trading practices because the agri-food sector is characterised by strong imbalances in the bargaining power between small and large operators, who sometimes impose conditions on their partners which are not in good faith and fair trade and which can also compromise the quality of the products offered to consumers. the directive we are discussing today will finally introduce a common minimum level of protection throughout the european union by prohibiting 16 unfair practices unilaterally imposed by one partner on another, such as late payment or last minute cancellations of orders. the importance of measures to strengthen cooperation between national authorities and the exchange of good practice should be emphasised in order to ensure the uniform application within the union of the rules and measures contained in the directive, aimed at protecting farmers and ensuring quality products.

i am not saying that the european parliament should be the only institution in the world to have a right to vote. the citizens' initiative. the effort to exhume it was an opportunity to give a first response to the challenges of the moment. the vast crisis of representative democracy, the offensive of the established powers against intermediary bodies, trade unions or ngos, the demand for direct or participatory democracy, a growing demand and risky only when it is not heard, as demonstrated by brexit and the yellow vest movement. the opportunity has been partly missed and the citizens are showing deep disappointment. the ice has been technically improved: the commission will be able to assess the success of the initiatives. but the power to legislate is monopolized by the commission and the collection of signatures is also in its hands. individual collection systems, although very effective, will be abolished. it's another slap in the face to the ngos. it's like we've built a more accessible smartphone, but it blocks calls. user-friendly not citizen-friendly. the citizen initiative is not killed, fortunately, but remains in a coma. the powers of the union are barricading themselves by closing the door to citizen participation at the very moment when they are glorifying the european demos. it is not a...
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too believe that by amending the regulation on the european citizens' initiative we have lost an opportunity to bring citizens closer to the european institutions. instead of strengthening an instrument designed to stem the democratic deficit which characterizes the present european union, the compromise reached between parliament and the council in some respects weakens this instrument. to date, within the limits imposed by the treaties, there is no obligation for the european commission to submit a legislative proposal on the subject of the citizens' initiative, even though it fulfils all the requirements of the regulation. if the compromise reached were to be confirmed, not only could the request coming directly from one million citizens still be ignored or circumvented, but the system of collecting individual signatures, managed directly by the organizers of an ice, which has been crucial to make the collection of signatures easier in feeding the debate and public awareness on the issues covered by an initiative, would even be canceled. we could also have strengthened this instrument in full respect of the treaties by increasing the number of hearings for each eci to three: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this would have given greater prominence to requests from citizens. the arrogance of those who believe that the best ideas for improving our union must necessarily come from the palaces of brussels has prevailed. the commission also remains a player and arbiter in this process. a role which allows it to choose the proposals to be submitted, thereby avoiding any accountability on the part of the citizens and giving them the feeling that the ice is a rigged game from the beginning. we can still make amends, and that is why we will ask the house tomorrow to vote on the amendments we have tabled to reopen the negotiations and to arrive at a text which finally gives value to this important instrument of direct democracy.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the mountain has given birth to a mouse again. the reform of the eic could have been a great opportunity to respond to a deep need for participation, to the expectations that the reform proposal had generated in european citizens. but once again, the text of the trilogue has frustrated those hopes, the hopes of those who were waiting for an ice that was finally effective and efficient. yes, a genuine intervention on the functioning of the eic would require an amendment of the treaties to put an end to the commission's absurd double role in verifying eligibility and deciding whether or not to follow up initiatives. but much more could be done, and above all, it could be opened up to civil society. no, in the face of positive technical adjustments, the text under voting is even a step backwards, giving the commission a further monopoly, the monopoly of using and managing the centralized platform instead of the platforms of the organizers, instead of the individual platforms, which had worked so well. well, i remember, in closing, the words of giorgio gaber: "freedom is participation". give greater freedom to civil society and give freedom to european citizens.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i bring to you tonight the voice of the people of the marche, the voice of those who trusted in 248 million euros of public money and in a priority axis of intervention specifically identified to support the earthquake-stricken areas of the marche. the erdf regional programme for the region, agreed with the european commission following the earthquakes of 2016 and 2017, provided that this money would go first to the 87 municipalities of the crater area, in order to provide support to the affected populations and activities in the territory. we all know how much we need it, but we're getting some disturbing news. it seems that the regional junta has decided to use a large part of those funds for interventions in the rest of the region. an example of all: of the 45 million euros allocated for strategic buildings, for healthcare buildings, 23 went outside the affected areas. we want to get to the bottom of this. i am sure that the commission will be able to answer this question in due course. it is not acceptable that the damage caused should be compounded by the mockery. we and the people of the marche want the truth.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with the paris agreement and the emissions trading system, the european union has set a clear course for reducing climate-altering emissions harmful to human health. in the city of taranto, in the south of italy, meanwhile, emissions of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons have increased by 105%. in taranto children are dying, schools are being closed, the right to education and health is being denied and people are being forced to choose between work and health, while the italian government is not following the implementation of the ilva agreement, is not implementing the institutional development contract, is not chairing the verification of environmental and employment data and is not actively using the resources available to the extraordinary administration. i ask the commission to support any technically sound proposal by the puglia region for the signing of a programme agreement for taranto, similar to the one signed with the calais region, which committed resources of one billion euro to promote the region's low-carbon economy.
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, first of all, i would like to thank president tajani for his letter, which the council received last week. i can assure you that we are committed to promoting gender balance. this is an important issue and the gender balance among the top staff of eu official financial bodies is also a key issue for the council. at the same time, the selection procedures are based on rules that we have to respect. the council has always acted – and will continue to act – in line with all the relevant provisions of eu law as regards its role in appointments. i would also expect all the other institutions involved to act within the legal framework and to do their utmost to promote gender balance. against this background, i was surprised that parliament is raising this issue specifically with the council. president tajani’s letter refers to legal acts that regulate appointments to three eu legal organs. these three bodies are the single supervisory board, the banking stakeholder group within the european banking authority, and the single resolution board. please allow me to clarify that the council is not involved in drawing up shortlists, nor in selecting successful candidates, for any of these three bodies. the shortlists for appointments to the single resolution board are provided by the commission. candidates for the single supervisory board are the responsibility of the european central bank. subsequently, for both of these boards, the european parliament decides on the successful contenders. the council’s role is limited to formally approving the selection made by parliament. as regards appointments to the european banking authority, the council has no role to play at all. regarding the selection of members of the ecb executive board, the council does indeed have a role in the selection procedure. i can assure you that we reiterate the importance of gender balance in each selection procedure and call on member states to propose female candidates. i trust that all eu institutions involved in preparing shortlists and selecting candidates observe and respect the principle of gender balance and that they will continue to do so in the future. as the presidency of the eu council, romania will continue to promote at european level the principle of gender balance, by facilitating debate on possible ways forward and advancing the legislative agenda, especially the negotiations on the directive on women on boards. important progress in this area of action has already been achieved through the consistent efforts of both the council and parliament in relation to the work-life balance directive, on which we have been able to finalise negotiations. we are determined to make our contribution to mainstreaming gender balance on the eu agenda in order to ensure a fair and equitable environment in our societies and within our labour markets.
member of the commission. – mr president, on behalf of the commission, including vice-president dombrovskis and commissioner moscovici, who are in brussels this morning at the ecofin council, i would like to thank you for this opportunity to exchange views on gender balance in the eu financial bodies. president juncker replied yesterday to the letter sent by president tajani on this matter. first of all, let me emphasise that this commission is fully committed to the principle of gender balance and has taken decisive action in this regard. 39.6% of middle and senior management is now female, up from 30% in november 2014. the number of female directors-general has increased from 14% to 30%, from five to 12. the number of female deputy directors- general has increased from 8% to 42% – it means from just three to 20. we also agree that women continue to be particularly under-represented in executive positions in the field of banking and financial services. women only account for about 15% of private executives. the under-representation of women can also be observed in the public sector entities in this field. women rarely make up more than a third of the governing bodies of most national central banks. the under-representation of women can be observed in a similar way in the applications for positions in eu agencies active in this field. on average, there are four to five times more male candidates than female candidates. on the specific cases you are debating today, i would like to stress that it follows from article 283/2 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union that the commission plays no role in the appointment of a new member of the executive board of the european central bank. as regards the european banking authority, the commission’s role is limited to assisting the board of supervisors in relation to the appointment of the chairperson of the european banking authority. for the single resolution board, currently chaired by a woman, the commission is indeed entrusted with providing the european parliament with a shortlist of candidates for the positions of chair, vice-chair and other members of the board. in line with the relevant regulation establishing the board, appointments are to be based on merit, skills, knowledge of banking and financial matters and on relevant expertise and experience. moreover, in line with article 56/4 of that regulation, candidates shall be chosen on the basis of an open selection procedure which must respect the principles of gender balance, experience and qualification. the commission is strongly in favour of supporting women with the necessary qualifications reaching top positions. we have taken this into account and rigorously respected the legal requirements in the selection procedures, and we have kept the european parliament informed at all stages of the process. in the cases of the chair of the european banking authority and the position of board member of the single resolution board, several candidates, including female candidates, failed to meet the eligibility criteria, often because they did not have the required minimum professional or senior management experience in the field of finance. we look forward to continuing the cooperation with this house on this very important matter. in the cases where the commission has a role in the process, the commission will continue to pay close attention to the issue of gender balance when composing shortlist of candidates for the eu financial services agencies.
i am not saying that we should not vote on the report, but that we should vote on the report. the problem is much more complex. in particular, as the commissioner has pointed out, we are faced with an under-representation of women in all top positions and at all levels, but certainly in private companies and in economic, financial and monetary institutions this under-representation is even higher. the problem is how to reverse this trend because, if there are no applications, i also understand that there is no other way to do it. in order to have applications, we must make it easier for women to pursue careers, especially in these institutions. we must tell girls that they can study economics and have a decent career, because if you tell them "look, if you study economics you will not be able to get ahead", nothing happens and in the end we do not have applications. i therefore ask the commission not only to adopt the right attitude but also to promote it at european level, to ask the member states to promote women's studies in technical, economic and scientific subjects at european level, if we are to have the right applications.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i do not want to waste a single second of my time, but i must do so to express the shame and even the indignation of hearing such shamefully backward voices in this parliament when they speak about women. i would say, however, that it is a defeat for us to close the legislature, once again, with the usual film. parliament is asking for it, but the commission admits it, commissioner jourová and the council are not listening, given this macroscopic absence of women in financial institutions. and i have to say that what is at stake is not an abstract principle of fairness that is worth defending, because sometimes principles have their foundation, even if abstract, but it is a discourse of fairness and it is a discourse of general interest. i don't think it's an act of goodwill, we're not here to ask for this or a gesture of attention: it is about recognising that the presence of women is inclusive of institutions, it strengthens them, it makes them more solid. i would just like to quote a study carried out by consob (the italian stock exchange regulator), a study which clearly shows, scientifically, that companies with women on the boards are better able to withstand the crisis and have better results... the prime minister of the slovak republic. mr president, mr vice-president of the european commission, before i make any final remarks, let me answer one question that has been raised here: what is slovakia's role? what is the role of the v4 countries, but what should be the role of all the leaders, all 28 and 27 countries of the european union? the main task, for me and my colleagues, must be to ensure that the people of our countries live well. that is the only clear objective with which we take over the leadership and the mandate and that is the only one with which we have to get up in the morning and go to sleep at night so that our citizens can live well and peacefully. and so, please, i always respect when we talk about someone or something, whether we have accomplished that goal first, so that we can then engage in uplifting and noble debates about some other matter. how can you force european union citizens to discuss some pseudo-topics unless they're living off a paycheck or they're out of a job or as seniors who collect their pension here, they live in poverty. let us first settle these matters and then we can bring into our debates the noble and great issues that, of course, belong to modern society, but unless we have done our homework that europeans will not be happy and live well, let us first do this homework. and i'm glad that people in our region are starting to live better than they did before, that our region is prospering economically, socially, culturally and socially, and i'm appropriately proud of that. and thank you for your words of support to all those who supported us and who also stood by the slovak republic in some comments that already exceed the powers of a particular member, sometimes even the standards of decent behavior. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me say that the european union will remain for slovakia, for us, a pillar of stability, freedom and prosperity. yes, i am aware of our weaknesses and mistakes, and also of the shortcomings of the european union, but we want to tackle them together as part of the further construction of the european project. we have common challenges economic, social, environmental, here in these areas, please let us seek unity together. i would like to stress once again that technological development is extremely important and that we must not fall behind the rest of the world. if we are talking about cohesion, please let's not bring politics into this and whether or not someone wants to continue in cohesion. cohesion was created to help us to eliminate the great regional disparities not only between member states but also within member states. cohesion should not be held hostage to political games. if we have to regret that the process of reducing regional disparities in the european union has stopped, it is a terrible news that it has stopped, so to debate what the future of cohesion should be is perverse. ladies and gentlemen, cohesion must be maintained as long as regional disparities remain as pronounced as they are. and until then, we are obliged to eliminate these regional differences between the different parts of europe, until we eliminate them completely, and then we can engage in a debate about whether or not cohesion should still exist in our european space. in conclusion, let us all try to be as close as possible to the citizens, to the people who will be deciding who will occupy these important seats in a few months' time. and i want to assure you that as prime minister of the slovak republic, i will do everything to ensure that slovakia continues to be a positive and constructive voice from central europe.

on behalf of the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, over the past year the negotiations on the association agreement with andorra, monaco and san marino have intensified. we aim to finalise discussions on the framework of the agreement by june. then it might take an additional two years for negotiations on the very high volume of eu legislation to be adopted by our partners. as rightly pointed out in the report by mr lópez aguilar, we enjoy excellent relations with these three small—sized states. the three countries are proud of their history and independence, yet we also have much in common. we are part of the same european family and it is only natural to seek an even closer partnership with them. we appreciate their desire to seek full integration into the internal market. andorra, monaco and san marino have made considerable efforts in the past years towards financial and economic recovery and towards preparations for the future association agreement. for example, they have already transposed, or are transposing, certain eu internal market rules. in line with parliament’s draft recommendations, we continue to encourage our partners to seek support from member states for the acquis takeover and implementation process. this will require strong administrative capacity, and cooperation with the eu countries can be of great help. we welcome the fact that the draft recommendations emphasise the importance of preserving the overall integrity and homogeneity of the internal market and of respect for the fundamental freedoms. we fully share parliament’s view and the union will not compromise on the main principles of the internal market. this is also our guideline in the negotiations with the united kingdom and switzerland. any agreement will fall within the limits set by these principles and rules, but within these limits there is certainly room for mediation that takes full account of the specific situation of our small—sized partners. in this respect, parliament’s recommendations are particularly welcome and timely. the european union seeks a comprehensive agreement with full access to the eu internal market, therefore covering all the four freedoms: movement of goods, services, persons and capital. the overall principles are always the same: same market, same rules. there is no such thing as partial integration. the four freedoms cannot be cherry-picked and separated from one another. for the same reason, the eu court of justice should have exclusive competence for the uniform interpretation and application of the agreement, including for last-resort dispute settlement. the commission, as guardian of the eu treaties, should be given competence to monitor the overall implementation of the agreement, including in the area of state aid. in line with parliament’s recommendations and with the eu treaties, we will look carefully into andorran, monegasque and san marinese requests for transitional arrangements on issues such as the right of establishment, the free movement of workers and the free provision of services. these requests should be duly justified and proportional. an association agreement would be a clear win—win situation and a further step towards a more united european continent.
i would like to thank mr lópez aguilar, my colleague and rapporteur. the association agreement between the european union, monaco, andorra and san marino is an important step in the construction of european integration, which today involves these three countries which have always been rooted in the history of europe but which have hitherto been outside the unitary project. in order to improve the text and to further strengthen cooperation, also through dialogue with my political family party, the party of socialists and democrats of san marino, i tabled and two amendments were adopted on crucial aspects such as scientific research and the interaction between the european parliament and the parliaments of the three states. the negotiations may provide an opportunity to put in place measures for investment in infrastructure of common interest, as well as academic research and scientific exchanges. it is also necessary to provide for regular hearings of national delegations to the european parliament throughout the negotiations. it is therefore essential that the integration of these three countries proceeds as fruitfully as possible, including in the areas where we may have disputes or mutual demands. in today's world, the more united we are in the european space, the stronger we all are.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the problem of non-performing loans has been widely discussed and identified as one of the problems needed to reduce risk in the european banking system. it should be noted that the main cause of the high stock of non-performing loans was the deep economic recession that hit several member states in the wake of the financial crisis, to which were added the negative effects of austerity policies. in some member states, it is also true that this main cause has been accompanied by poorly transparent credit practices, mismanagement or insufficient prudence. in this respect, several measures have already been taken, both at national and european level, and this is resulting in a significant decrease in the level of non-performing loans. the text we have agreed - and i would like to thank my colleague esther de lange for her cooperation, which has brought us to the end of such a delicate legislative procedure in record time - has two main objectives: on the one hand, to strengthen measures to prevent the excessive accumulation of non-performing loans, and on the other hand to do so by avoiding negative incentives from the point of view of the ability to support the economy or even from the point of view of debtors, who would of course be negatively affected by an excessive downward selling of non-performing loans. what are the main points of the agreement reached with the council? firstly, we have decided to apply this prudential backstop only to new claims arising from new loans, in line with the council's action plan, which called for this. this is logical, because it takes a sufficient period of time to adapt to the new rules, from an accounting and prudential point of view. the second element is that we have in the text a correct and fair balance of reserve levels for the banks. in particular, unlike the commission proposal, provisioning for secured and unsecured loans starts only after two or three years respectively, thus avoiding the risk that prudential provisions will add to the capital contraction caused by the recession, creating a procyclical effect, with negative effects on credit provisioning and the real economy. we have also eliminated the potentially negative (or perverse) incentives in the commission's proposal which would have accelerated the liquidation of firms which were only temporarily unable to repay their loans, but which were actually solvent, with negative consequences not only for the companies themselves, especially small and mediumsized enterprises, but also for economic growth and employment. last but not least, i would also like to mention an element we have introduced, namely a more favourable prudential treatment for those non-performing loans which are bought on the secondary market by other credit institutions, so as to avoid an unfair penalty for specialised operators and at the same time provide a higher level of protection for consumers, smes and all other debtors, since these institutions are subject to strict controls and regulations. in conclusion, this is a balanced text which helps us to take another important step forward in reducing the risks of the banking sector, while avoiding negative consequences for the real economy and consumers. that is why we call for support for the text.
on behalf of the efdd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i myself and my group are very concerned about the measures that will be applied with this package on non-performing loans, firstly because the impact study has not been done, and therefore the impacts on the housing market and the impact on consumers, businesses and european citizens are all to be checked, because incentivising the sale of non-performing loans in a short time, compared to sound management that banks could do internally, also involves a speculative mechanism. we know that there are several funds that have also advised the european central bank and the ssm during the stress tests, which are very interested in getting their hands on these packages of nonperforming loans. i would not want the houses, the real estate, the assets of the citizens to go into the hands of these speculators. and since we are talking about risk reduction, i wonder where the risk reduction on derivatives, for example, that the big european commercial banks are carrying is and when this blessed risk sharing will come. we look forward to a risk-sharing arrangement on the guarantee of joint deposits.

member of the commission. – madam president, let me first thank the european parliament, the committee on international trade (inta), the rapporteur, mr christofer fjellner, and all the shadow rapporteurs for the attention, work and time that you have invested into this report on the implementation of the generalised scheme of preferences (gsp) regulation. it is a welcome initiative, as it comes at a moment when we are assessing the impact and effectiveness of the current gsp regulation and what possible improvements we can bring to a successor gsp scheme. the eu has had the gsp scheme since 1971. the primary objective, as set out in the wto enabling clause, has always been to assist vulnerable developing countries in their efforts to reduce poverty and integrate into the world economy. the european union’s gsp has undergone several transformations over the decades. a major reform of the gsp took place in 2012, with three main objectives: first, to contribute to poverty eradication by expanding exports from the countries most in need. this was done by substantially reducing the number of beneficiaries and focusing gsp preferences on the most vulnerable economies. secondly, to promote sustainable development and good governance. we increased the attractiveness of gsp+ and enhanced the gsp+ monitoring of effective implementation of core international conventions related to human rights, labour rights, protection of the environment and good governance. thirdly, to better protect the eu’s financial and economic interests. in this respect, the safeguard mechanism was overhauled to make it more accessible to eu industry. we are now five years into the implementation of the gsp regulation and i am pleased to note that overall, the european parliament and the commission share the assessment that the gsp regulation is successful in meeting its objectives. exports from the more vulnerable economies have expanded substantially, which can contribute to poverty eradication. gsp, and in particular gsp+, is also contributing positively to furthering human and labour rights in beneficiary countries. we agree with your view that trade policy, including gsp, must also be part of eu efforts to fight for values enshrined in the eu treaties, such as democracy, rule of law and human rights. trade policy does not and cannot do this on its own or in isolation. we take great care to ensure coherence between all eu external policies. for example, we ensure that gsp+ dialogues and bilateral human rights dialogues with beneficiary countries reinforce each other, thus increasing the eu’s leverage to push for progress. as the commission’s biannual reports on gsp+ implementation attest, we are seeing progress in all beneficiary countries. however, many problematic issues remain and we will continue to engage closely and firmly with beneficiary countries. i would like to touch on an issue that is very important to us, namely, transparency in trade policy. in the implementation of the gsp regulation, we make considerable efforts to ensure a transparent and inclusive process. we consult civil society in the european union and in beneficiary countries on a very regular basis and we are always open to their input, which we greatly value. we do not always share their views on what course of action should be taken at a specific point in time, but this should not be taken to mean that we do not listen to civil society. let me be very clear: the commission will not hesitate to take its responsibilities when it comes to warranted cases of serious and systematic violation of fundamental rights. our actions in relation to cambodia and myanmar clearly demonstrate this. in this respect, i agree with you that withdrawing gsp must be a last-resort measure. we must now start work on the new gsp scheme that will take effect when the current one expires on 31 december 2023. as we have seen in the mid—term evaluation of the gsp regulation, it is working well overall and this should be the starting point. your report and resolution contains several proposals that we will examine carefully. the next immediate step in this process is to launch an impact assessment to help guide our work on a new gsp regulation. this will include a wide-ranging public consultation. we count on working closely with you on this important endeavour.
